        The attention of the soccer world will be fixed on London to start the week, where a months-old question will finally be answered: Who's going to win the Ballon d'Or? I'm Pardeep Cattry with a lookahead to Monday's ceremony, plus a preview of what's to come as action resumes in the EFL Cup.
   
   

    📺 Footy fixAll times U.S./EasternMonday, Oct. 26🇫🇷 Ligue 1: Paris Saint-Germain vs. Lyon, 3:30 p.m. ➡️ beIN Sports🏆 Ballon d'Or ceremony, 4 p.m. ➡️ DAZNTuesday, Oct. 27🇮🇹 Serie A: Roma vs. Cagliari, 3:45 p.m. ➡️ Paramount+🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 EFL Cup: Fleetwood Town vs. Arsenal, 4 p.m. ➡️ Paramount+⚽ The Forward Line🏆 Surprises in store at the Ballon d'Or?Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo may no longer be the frontrunners for the Ballon d'Or, but their decades-long command over soccer's most prestigious individual accolade still colors the way we all look at the award. The air of mystery that should be a fixture in the run-up to an awards show still feels foreign, the ability to gauge the eventual winner a fresh challenge for many. That's especially true this year, particularly on the men's side, where none of the usual indicators apply.
A handful of deserving players make up the list of nominees once again, but none fit the prototype of an eventual Ballon d'Or winner, rightly or wrongly. The award often goes to the best player on a team that won the biggest prize on offer in the last year, a path that would lead you straight to Spain's golden ball winner, Rodri. The midfielder hardly feels like a slam-dunk pick after spending much of last season building his form following an ACL injury, which might lead you to a member of Paris Saint-Germain's UEFA Champions League-winning team. Vitinha, the Portuguese midfielder, might actually have a shot but there are buzzier names in the mix that are equally worthy. The favorite might actually be someone else entirely – Harry Kane, the England captain and Bayern Munich talisman who has steadily established himself as his generation's greatest goalscorer over the years. Here's James Benge on Kane's case in the final batch of Ballon d'Or power rankings.Benge: "Perhaps it was the endings to his tilts at the Champions League and World Cup that make it so hard to lock in on Kane as the best player in the world last season. If the 33-year-old really were that good, would he not have found a way to bend the biggest games in his direction? That semifinal against Argentina in particular was one of those late-summer Kane games where he looks too leggy to impact the game either in the penalty area or the midfield roles he drops into, usually with such success. That's one game, though. There are another 64 where he was frequently spectacular. A remarkable 73 goals for club and country is the sort of output that belonged back in Messi's prime years. The absolute biggest game may not have gone his way, but Kane was unforgettable against the Ivory Coast, thrilling in both legs against PSG and incisive in putting Real Madrid to the sword. Then there are the Bundesliga numbers. Gaudy output is the baseline for a Bayern striker against domestic opposition but still the only players to have bettered Kane's 36 goals in 31 league games are Gerd Muller and Robert Lewandowski. The former won the Ballon d'Or, the latter probably would have if it had been awarded in 2020. There is no reason why Kane should not get it this time."There is no obvious candidate on the women's side, either, though Alexia Putellas might just be the favorite if the usual patterns apply. The voting body will be inclined to select someone from Barcelona's UEFA Women's Champions League-winning side and with three-time Ballon d'Or winner Aitana Bonmati out of the running after dealing with a broken leg last season, Putellas playing a central role with eight goals and six assists in Europe before leaving for London City Lionesses in the summer. She is one of eight members of that squad among the list of nominees, the list of 30 an eclectic selection of some of the world's best players. The NWSL's nominees include Temwa Chawinga, the league's back-to-back MVP with the Kansas City Current and the headliner for a Malawi side that made a run to the Women's Africa Cup of Nations, and U.S. women's national team standout Rose Lavelle, who scored the game-winner for Gotham FC in last year's NWSL Championship.📺 Tune In What's on CBS Sports Golazo Network☀️ Morning Footy (Weekdays 10 a.m. to 12 p.m.): Join Golazo Network as it helps fans get their day started on the right foot on the network's flagship morning show with highlights, interviews and the biggest soccer storylines. Morning Footy is also available in podcast form, so you'll never have to miss an episode.3️⃣ Attacking Third: The leading women's soccer podcast and social brand is now a live studio show. title: How will CFP expansion affect bowl games? Bowl Season boss optimistic amid uncertain future - CBS Sports
description: The future of college football's bowl games rests with the conferences and their television partners, and neither has said what it wants
body:
The future of college football's bowl games rests with the conferences and their television partners, and neither has said what it wants as the College Football Playoff closes in on 24 teams, Bowl Season executive director Nick Carparelli told CBS Sports.Roughly six bowl executives gathered in Irving, Texas, last week to discuss the future of college football's bowl season. They represented a cross-section of Group of Six and Power Four bowl games. Some of them have spent decades in a business that, for most of that time, renewed itself every few years with little more than a handshake and a few signatures.That era is over, and they know it. Now they're trying to prepare for a postseason being redrawn around them by people who haven't finished the blueprint.The College Football Playoff is on the verge of doubling its field to 24 teams starting in 2027 after reaching a handshake agreement, according to multiple reports. Nearly $350 million will be added to the $1.3 billion deal with ESPN, which is expected to run six years, the typical length for the CFP contract and the separate deals among the Bowl Season's 35 bowl games serving 10 conferences. 
The bowls' agreements with their conference partners, which ran six years to mirror the CFP cycle, expire after this season, and so do their television deals. CFP expansion will pull 12 more teams out of the bowl pool, nearly all of them from Power Four conferences. The first two rounds are expected to be played on campuses, with the New Year's Six bowls hosting the quarterfinals and semifinals."I would say that it's too soon to predict the number of bowl games moving forward," Carparelli told CBS Sports. "But I think it's safe to say that, as a complementary part of college football's postseason, there will still be more teams playing in bowl games than are participating in the playoff."He added: "The bowl system is not going anywhere."The bowl system might not disappear, but it could change drastically.A postseason waiting on directionHow many games survive is the question nobody will answer. The bowl lineup already turned over this year. The LA Bowl and Detroit's GameAbove Sports Bowl are gone, replaced by the new Puerto Rico Bowl and the returning Poinsettia Bowl.
That makes 35 bowl games for a system that is still a ratings win for ESPN, though conferences worry about dwindling returns as the playoff expands to 24 teams. Michigan and Texas drew 9.1 million viewers in last season's Citrus Bowl. Both would have been playoff teams in a 24-team field, leaving bowls like the Citrus to fill premium slots with lesser teams.But live sports remain a major ratings win for networks, making bowl games valuable inventory. Non-playoff bowls on ESPN's networks averaged 3.1 million viewers last season, up 13% from the year before. It was the highest non-playoff average since the 2015-16 season.
Only 22.8% of regular-season games through Week 7 this year have eclipsed 3.1 million viewers, according to Nielsen TV ratings for trackable college football games. Only 3.5% of games have drawn ratings equal to or greater than last season's Citrus Bowl."Even with 24 in the playoff, there's still nearly 60 deserving teams that may want a place to play," Carparelli said. "It's been proven that fans still love watching those games."Bowl games are clearly valuable, particularly during the doldrums of December, but will the product be watered down if 12 additional playoff games pull viewers' attention?
That's a question for conference, bowl and media executives to answer before the 2027 season.ESPN's direct relationship with the system also helps steer the future. ESPN Events owns and operates 17 bowl games. Carparelli said those games "are a really important part of bowl season" and that ESPN Events as an enterprise "remains very profitable for ESPN.""So I think we should expect to see the majority of those games continue," he said.
Carparelli said ESPN Events has shown no hesitation as the network takes on more playoff games, costing nearly a quarter billion dollars annually."Absolutely not," Carparelli said. "Quite the opposite. You know, if you think about it, December and January is an exciting time of year in college football. And with the expanded playoff, you're going to have four or five rounds that are spaced 10 days apart. I don't think the television networks or the fans want to go 10 days with no college football at the height of the season."The bowls are waiting on the conferences. The conferences are waiting on the playoff. Once the format is final, Carparelli said, he expects serious conversations before the end of the year.
"It's hard for any of the conferences to turn their focus on what they want next from the bowl system until that's done," Carparelli said. "But we have great indication from them and great conversations that they are ready to talk about opportunities beyond the CFP, ASAP, after any formal announcement is made."Reimagining bowl seasonThe Power Four conferences have already floated one idea.Yahoo! Sports reported in March on a proposal shared with high-level administrators: a consortium of 10 bowls pitting Power Four programs against each other, untethered from traditional conference affiliations, with the conferences controlling television rights instead of the bowls and potentially selling them on the open market. ESPN was part of the proposal. The top 10 non-playoff bowls, all matching Power Four teams, paid out more than $50 million combined last season, according to the report.Carparelli confirmed to CBS Sports the concept came from the leagues."That's a very interesting concept," he said. "It's a concept that the conferences presented to us to think about. And our membership is generally accepting of that idea."
The ideas don't stop there."I think there's definitely a lot of creative thinking around maximizing bowl game matchups after the playoff selections are made, maximizing geography, maximizing quality of teams, maximizing rivalries," Carparelli said.Even the traditional New Year's Eve and New Year's Day slots could move. Conference tie-ins to specific bowl sites might also be out the window.The Group of Six conferences have not pitched a similar package, but they remain engaged.
For the people who actually stage the games, the cost of waiting is measured in sponsorships and gate receipts.The longer a decision drags, "the more challenging it gets to figure out funding mechanisms," said Scott Ramsey, president and CEO of the Music City Bowl. For his game, that means broadcast partners, sponsorships and gate revenue. The Music City Bowl's SEC-Big Ten matchup is wide open once its contract expires this year."Certainly the value proposition, you know, kind of shifted to viewership instead of attendance, because you did see, you know, some drop in attendance," Ramsey said.
Bowl Season has run its own projections for the next cycle, Carparelli said, but "it's just speculation and is completely dependent on what the conferences ultimately are going to want." Asked whether the number of bowl games drastically changed from 35 in those studies, he declined to comment."There is every indication that there is a need and a desire for more postseason opportunities beyond the playoff," Carparelli said. "It's just a matter of figuring out what that looks like once the dust settles."

        It was nice to have a week without a ton of injuries -- and with a ton of scoring. Going into Monday night, just nine teams failed to score 20 points. And honestly, the number of teams with over 20 points should have been higher if not for some weird flubs and questionable calls in the Packers-Lions showdown.  And how about some props for the tight ends on National Tight Ends Day?! Going into Monday night, there have been 63 instances of a tight end scoring at least 11.5 half-PPR points. That's almost 30% more than the 50 through seven weeks last season. Those big lugs are making their presence felt! Our daily Fantasy Football Today podcast includes a must-watch Sunday night livestream every single week after the late-afternoon games end. It's our chance to react to what happened across the league and give an initial prognosis on what will happen moving forward. It's a great place to celebrate ... or commiserate.So while there are far more than two winners and two losers from this week's games, here are the winners and losers I gave on our show. Please keep in mind: I never share "winners" who are obvious studs (like Jaxon Smith-Njigba), and I never share "losers" who are obvious bench guys (like Chris Godwin).
Week 7 Fantasy WinnersBrowns RB Quinshon Judkins
Quinshon Judkins was started in 63% of leagues and put up over 100 total yards and two touchdowns despite playing only 52% of the snaps. The snap share has nowhere to go but up and thus could be an opportunity for Judkins to carve out a larger role for the 5-2 Cleveland Browns. They're continuing to find ways to win games. And as my colleague Jamey Eisenberg pointed out on our Sunday show, I liked Judkins for his receiving potential against the Titans, and he made his numbers as a rusher. That's actually more evidence that we can expect Judkins' receiving profile to eventually matter. Titans RB Tony Pollard
Started in only 49% of leagues, Tony Pollard had his first game with more than 13.6 PPR fantasy points. He almost tripled that number with his three-score smash of the Browns. The Titans' record is a gross 1-6, but four of their past five losses have been by one score. Point is, they're competitive, and Pollard can keep earning touches in their games because they're not getting blown out. Their upcoming schedule -- at Cincy, bye, Jacksonville, at Dallas, at Jacksonville and Washington -- is rough. So you could take this opportunity to sell high on Pollard. Or, see if the Titans sell high on Pollard and move him to a contender. If they do, then his value could shoot up immensely as he'd theoretically be part of a better offense. He's in the final year of his contract, so it would make sense for the Titans to get something for Pollard before the trade deadline between Weeks 9 and 10. Week 7 Fantasy LosersJets WR Garrett Wilson
The threats to Garrett Wilson's target volume are legitimate. With other receivers involved and Breece Hall on his way back, we may rarely see the crazy-high target volume from Wilson on a weekly basis that we hoped for. As an example, Wilson had just nine targets in his past two games combined. It must be mentioned that the Jets schedule is incredible from Week 8 through 12, then after their bye it's nasty. His next big game should be the off-ramp that fantasy managers might want to look for in order to avoid the target crunch he seems destined to deal with. 
For a deeper dive into the full game-by-game breakdown and additional start/sit advice, check out the full episode on the Week 7 Winners & Losers Fantasy Football Recap.

title: LeBron James explains why he doesn't want to play a 'sustainable role' at center for the 76ers - CBS Sports
description: With Joel Embiid out, LeBron started at center on Sunday in the Sixers' first loss of the season

With Joel Embiid out, LeBron started at center on Sunday in the Sixers' first loss of the season

        When LeBron James joined the Philadelphia 76ers, he highlighted his versatility as a reason the fit could work. "The luxury of my game is that I can do everything," James said at 76ers media day. "Literally, I can do everything." Of course, just because he can do everything doesn't mean he wants to. There is one job, at least thus far, he'd prefer to hand off to a teammate: playing center.Considering Joel Embiid's lengthy injury history and the season-long loss of Ariel Hukporti to a torn Achilles, front-court depth is a notable concern for Philadelphia. On Sunday, Embiid missed his first game of the season due to plantar fasciitis management, and part of the replacement plan involved playing James at center. It's a role he can take in small doses, but not one he hopes to maintain for much more than that."Well, shit, we got an MVP over there. I'm not here to have a sustainable role at the 5," James said after Sunday's loss to the Detroit Pistons, the Sixers' first defeat of the season. "You got Joel Embiid on the team. ... If I was to say I was signed here to have a sustainable role at the 5, I don't think none of us would actually want that. I can do it, but... we have [Embiid]."The very early numbers support the notion that James is best served playing elsewhere. James has played 50 possessions at center thus far this season, according to Cleaning the Glass, and the Sixers have a -10 net rating within those minutes. The historical numbers are a bit more complicated. James didn't start playing center consistently until the 2021-22 season, and he did so mostly out of roster necessity. The trends are about what you'd expect: James-at-center lineups tend to be very good offensively and very weak defensively.

This will be LeBron's age-42 season. He simply is not at the same stage of his career physically that he was when he started playing center more frequently with the Los Angeles Lakers. Keeping him healthy is the priority for Philadelphia, and center is the most physically demanding position on the court for James. That, more than anything, is the reason to minimize these stretches.When Embiid is healthy, that's fully doable. He was not on Sunday, nor were Hukporti, Dominick Barlow, Jabari Walker or Tacko Fall. "We've only got about three guys left that can possibly play the 5," 76ers head coach Nick Nurse said before the game. James was one of them.
As James said back on media day, he can play center mostly because he can play anywhere. An emergency situation like Sunday hopefully isn't the norm. But the reality of employing Embiid on a supermax contract is that affording reliable backups is almost impossible and he's going to miss time due to injury. If his durability is as much of a concern this season as it has been in the past, the Sixers may not have much choice but to play James at center more than he likes, at least until they can pursue more depth closer to the trade deadline.

title: Chiefs have a Harrison Butker problem: Andy Reid says KC kicker 'gotta fix it' - CBS Sports

Butker missed two field goals during Kansas City's Week 7 loss to the Seahawks on Sunday

        The Kansas City Chiefs may have a kicking problem on their hands. Longtime placekicker Harrison Butker hasn't been as sharp as he has been at times during his tenure with KC, and the warts were all too apparent in the team's 20-3 loss to the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday night. Butker failed to connect on two of his three field goal attempts, with each of those misses proving to be massive gut punches and momentum killers. The first came just before halftime. While it was a sluggish start for the Kansas City offense as it faced a lethal Seattle defense, it had an opportunity to cut into the 10-0 deficit just before the break thanks to a 65-yard interception return by corner Nohl Williams. After a 4-yard gain by Kenneth Walker inched them a little closer, Butker trotted out for a 58-yard attempt, but it didn't have the leg. 
While Butker connected on a 50-yard field goal in the third quarter, he again failed to come up in the clutch for the Chiefs later in the second half. With just under nine minutes to play in regulation, Butker came out for a 45-yard attempt, which would've brought the Chiefs within a touchdown (and extra point) of tying the game. Instead, it was wide right, with an emphasis on wide. 
"He's been one of the most consistent kickers in football," head coach Andy Reid said of Butker postgame. "He's off a bit, so gotta fix it."
Will Butker's troubles affect Chiefs' postseason aspirations?Mostly, Butker's struggles have come from long range. This season, he's connecting on just 33.3% of kicks from 50-plus yards (2-of-6). Since the start of last season, Butker is 7-of-15 from 50-plus yards (50%). Harrison Butker's field goal attemptsInside 50From 50+20269-10 (90%)2-6 (33.3%)202528-30 (93.3%)5-8 (62.5%)202419/20 (95%)2-5 (40%)While the long-range issues have been a big chunk of the problem, Butler has also missed five PATs since the start of last season. Combined with 10 missed field goals, Butler's 15 missed kicks since the start of last season are the most in the NFL, per CBS Sports Research. That's 35 points the Chiefs have lost because of Butker's misses during that time span. As Reid cautioned, Butker has to fix these issues and be a more reliable option in the kicking game for Kansas City, especially as it pushes toward getting back into the playoffs. Because KC missed the postseason last year, Butker's kicking problems haven't reached that make-or-break portion of the calendar. Over his past two playoff runs (2023 and 2024), Butker has been perfect, netting all 15 of his field goals (two from 50-plus) and all 13 of his extra points. 
That predates these recent struggles, however, and if they persist this time around, it could very well be the difference between the Chiefs getting back to the Super Bowl and ultimately hoisting another Lombardi Trophy or not.

title: Garrett Wilson explains heated Jets sideline exchange, denies yelling at Geno Smith - CBS Sports

The star receiver acknowledged that he was unhappy with New York's red-zone play calls during an animated conversation

        The New York Jets hit a potential rock bottom Sunday after falling to the previously winless Miami Dolphins, dropping the franchise to 2-5 on the year. Amid that divisional upset at home, patience had seemingly started to wear thin, specifically when it comes to wideout Garrett Wilson. During the broadcast, CBS cameras captured the Jets star pass catcher having an animated conversation on the sideline. From the looks of things, Wilson appears to be yelling towards a huddle of Geno Smith and passing-game coordinator Seth Ryan. When asked about it postgame, Wilson said he was not directing his frustrations at Smith and acknowledged he was upset with the red-zone play calls. "We were collaborating," said Wilson, via ESPN. "I don't even think I was talking to Geno. I think we were both heated, but not at each other at all. We were just disappointed with how we were playing up to that point and wanted to be a little more aggressive. That's what that was."For his part, Smith also didn't think Wilson was directing anything towards him. 
"He might have been yelling, but I don't think he was yelling at me," he said.
In the loss, Wilson -- the highest-paid player on the team -- saw only three targets, catching two passes for 26 yards. That said, Smith was able to find some success through the air via different pass-catching outlets like rookie wideout Omar Cooper Jr. (five catches, 115 yards receiving and a touchdown) and tight end Mason Taylor (five catches, 62 yards receiving and two touchdowns). Still, the offense is at its best when Wilson is involved. "I think we can all do a better job of finding ways to get him more targets and more touches," Smith said. "But the ball has to go where it goes based on coverage."Through seven games, Wilson has caught 37 of his team-high 51 targets for 444 receiving yards and three receiving touchdowns. Over the last two games, he's seen nine targets. Smith and Wilson were reportedly seen in the locker room having a conversation after coming out of the shower and walking to their lockers. Wilson said the talk was focused on finding a resolution. 
"Just trying to figure out how we can fix where we're at right now, wanting to get it in our hands and make a difference and try to win these games that we feel like we're a better team -- and we're not," he said."Like I've said before, I want it in my hands to try and make an impact. So that's all we were talking about, just putting it in our hands and how we can make that happen, being aggressive throughout and keeping ourselves out of those situations so we can win these games."The Jets have lost two straight and will look to stop the skid and get Wilson back on track next week as they host a Las Vegas Raiders team that has surrendered 35.8 points per game over their current four-game losing streak.

title: Packers blast officiating after loss to Lions: 'It's bull----' and 'f---ing up the games' - CBS Sports
description: Safety Xavier McKinney unloaded on the referees following a 20-17 defeat, calling out phantom penalties that kept
body:
Safety Xavier McKinney unloaded on the referees following a 20-17 defeat, calling out phantom penalties that kept key drives alive for Detroit and that drew criticism from Tom Brady
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 26, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:28 am ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Green Bay Packers had their three-game win streak snapped on Sunday, as Jared Goff and the rival Detroit Lions defeated them, 20-17. While Packers kicker Trey Smack missed a 35-yard field goal with 3:25 remaining in the fourth quarter, setting the stage for a Lions' game-winning drive, there were several questionable officiating calls that played into Detroit's favor as well.In all, Green Bay was penalized eight times for 81 yards. Many of those calls, though, were called into question and outright blasted by the Packers. Safety Xavier McKinney felt it was necessary to make it clear how disgusted he was with the calls on Sunday, calling them "bullshit" after the game. "I don't know how the NFL's going to treat it, but I'm not a big fan of the refs right now," McKinney said. "I don't think it's great officiating, if I'm being completely honest. I think it's bullshit a lot of the times."One of the most controversial calls was a roughing-the-passer penalty on Karl Brooks with 2:45 remaining in the fourth quarter, adding 15 yards to an 18-yard gain by Sam LaPorta. Even Fox commentator and legendary quarterback Tom Brady couldn't hide his disgust. "What is that? There's no way," Brady said. "That's definitely not roughing the passer."
Many of the questionable calls involved personal foul penalties that either seemed like a stretch or were completely unclear. Earlier in the third quarter, the Lions were given an automatic first down when Brenton Cox Jr. was called for roughing the passer after attempting to catch himself while fighting through a block. He did put his hands on Goff, but did not extend or make any illegal action that could have qualified as roughing the passer. At least, that's what Brady and rules analyst Dean Blandino believe. 
"I don't know," Cox said about his penalty, per ESPN. "I'm trying to give you a good answer, but it's disappointing that these are veteran guys -- I'm not trying to go after the refs -- well-informed guys, and I feel like you've got to know the difference between what's intentional and what's not."In the third quarter, Devonte Wyatt was flagged for unnecessary roughness after he took down Amon-Ra St. Brown, who got up with the ball and tried to run as if the play was still alive. Wyatt slung St. Brown down, who accidentally cleated an official in the gut. The ref threw the flag from his back.
"There was no whistle blown, and the guy continued to run, and our guy didn't hear a whistle -- he continued to play too, and then we get called for a penalty," said Packers head coach Matt LaFleur after the game. "So I don't know. They were trying to tell me the play was obviously dead. I'm like, 'How do you know if you don't hear a whistle?' So I don't know if you guys heard a whistle. I did not hear a whistle."Overall, LaFleur didn't want to address the penalties. He knew he would be subject to fines if he lashed out for the officials' rough afternoon. "I don't even want to comment on any of the penalties," LaFleur said. "I just -- it is what it is. You got to play above it, and I thought there were some tough calls, but it is what it is." 
McKinney, who said he didn't care about being fined by the NFL for complaining about the officiating, argued the phantom penalties killed momentum for the Packers, and that the calls simply don't make sense. "It's annoying even talking about it because these are critical drives throughout the game, and we might have a drive where we're getting stops but you're calling penalties, and it's like, this is not a penalty," McKinney said. "To me, it just don't really make any sense, and it's killing our momentum, it's killing our drives, and it's kind of f---ing up the games, if I'm being honest."I would rather get fined and try to help my team out because I see what's going on, and it's killing us."
Packers cornerback Keisean Nixon also sounded off on the officiating, saying he felt the calls were clearly one-sided. Calls that went against the Packers could have also easily gone against the Lions, he thought.  "We can't really leave it in the refs' hands, it can always go both ways, they clearly don't like Jordan Love. They don't throw nothing on him ever," Nixon said, via WLUK-TV Fox 11.On the first play of the fourth quarter, Love was called for intentional grounding despite tight end Tucker Kraft clearly being the intended target. Referee Alex Moore told PFWA pool reporter Ben Raven that it was called since the pass did not reach the line of scrimmage, but Brady flat-out said this was "definitely not grounding" on the telecast.
In what is good news for the Packers, they will have to shift their focus to Week 8 quickly, as they host the Carolina Panthers on "Thursday Night Football."

Miranda Lambert is the 30th Red Kettle Kickoff halftime performer

        The Dallas Cowboys have a long history of playing on Thanksgiving, and this year they will host the Philadelphia Eagles in an NFC East clash. The tradition of playing on Turkey Day also includes a special halftime show performance.This year, Miranda Lambert will take the AT&T Stadium stage between the football action on Thursday, Nov. 26, the Cowboys announced on Sunday. The game and halftime show will be broadcast on Fox, with fans at home able to enjoy the music as well. Kickoff is set for 4:30 p.m. ET. 
This marks the 30th consecutive Red Kettle Kickoff halftime performance, which marks the start of The Salvation Army's annual Red Kettle Campaign. The campaign encourages fans to give back and support local programs to help those in need."There's something special about how music brings people together, especially when it's to spread joy and hope to families who need it most," Lambert said in the press release. "The Salvation Army and the Dallas Cowboys have built an incredible tradition with the Red Kettle Kickoff, and I can't wait to be back home in Texas this Thanksgiving to help carry it forward."
Lambert is a successful country artist and songwriter, with 31 Grammy nominations, three Grammy wins, 40 Academy of Country Music Awards and 14 Country Music Association Awards. She is the most-awarded artist in the Academy of Country Music's history. The singer released her most recent album, "Crisco," earlier this month, continuing her streak of 11 consecutive top 10 country albums.Her resume also includes being a New York Times bestselling author and a non-profit co-founder. Her MuttNation Foundation has raised over $15 million, encouraging shelter pet adoption, supporting rescue organizations across the nation and helping shelters after natural disasters. The Cowboys have played on Thanksgiving since 1966, with the exception of 1975 and 1977, when the St. Louis Cardinals were given the holiday game. Last year, the Cowboys beat the Kansas City Chiefs 31-28 on Thanksgiving. The last time they lost on the holiday was in 2021, an overtime defeat against the Las Vegas Raiders. 
The Cowboys currently sit at 2-4 and are in third place in the NFC East. They play on Monday night in a divisional game against the 2-4 Philadelphia Eagles.

title: College basketball coaching hot seat: Five coaches under pressure entering a pivotal 2026-27 season - CBS Sports
description: It's not the best place to be before a game has even been played, but these five coaches already have a lot to pr
body:
It's not the best place to be before a game has even been played, but these five coaches already have a lot to prove to save their jobs
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 26, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:28 am ET
                        
                •
            
            6 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        CBS Sports' annual list of the Top 25 And 1 college basketball coaches was published on Monday. It's a list shaped by a vote of college basketball writers and analysts and filled with Naismith Memorial Hall of Famers and future Naismith Memorial Hall of Famers.It's a nice list to be on, obviously.This list, not so much.Because this is our annual list of five coaches on the hot seat -- a list that, to be clear, should not be interpreted as a prediction of five coaches who will lose their jobs during or after the 2026-27 season. That's not what this is. Rather, this is simply a list of five coaches who likely need good seasons relative to their program's expectations to ensure they still have their jobs in April. It's a list of five men living with real job-pressure. Sure, they're all multimillionaires who will receive lucrative buyouts if they're removed -- and that's certainly better than the alternative. But getting publicly scrutinized and criticized on the way to what amounts to a pink slip is never fun, no matter a person's net worth.Ask any rich/fired coach.
        
            
                College basketball's NIL arms race, from $5M to $25M+: Breaking down roster values, spending tiers for 2026-27
                
                    Matt Norlander                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
They might ultimately adjust to not working and actually enjoy the new lifestyle -- and that buyout money is always nice. But the journey from here to there, from a hot seat list in October to a termination in March, is often a brutal ride that takes an awful toll on coaches and their families.The good news here is that every man on this list has a reasonable chance to coach his way off of it -- at least temporarily. One of them likely will. Maybe more. For now, let's just wish them all good luck.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Penny Hardaway | MemphisRecord at school: 175-87 entering ninth seasonLast NCAA Tournament appearance at school: 2025No program has fallen further over the past 20 years than Memphis -- and I don't even think it's mostly Hardaway's fault. The changing landscape of the sport, combined with every other program that mattered leaving the American Conference while Memphis remains in a league that ranked 10th nationally last season at KenPom, has played a bigger role. Either way, no traditional-aged college student can remember the Tigers on a Sweet 16 run, considering the last one came three coaches ago and way back in 2009. The byproduct of all of this is season-ticket sales dropping below 2,000 in an NBA arena, and a reality where sports fans in Memphis have gone from knowing every player on the roster to basically none. The Tigers finished 13-19 last season in a year that doubled as the worst for the program since 1970.
It's gotten bad.And even if it's not all Hardaway's fault, it is all happening on his watch, and he will not be back for Year 10 unless his team performs like what it is -- specifically the best-funded program in its conference, and by a significant margin. Hardaway only has one conference championship in eight years. If that's still true after nine, barring extenuating circumstances, it'll be difficult for the program's greatest alum to overcome.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Porter Moser | OklahomaRecord at school: 95-75 entering sixth seasonLast NCAA Tournament appearance at school: 2025Moser is a good coach with a Final Four on his Wikipedia page thanks to his time at Loyola Chicago and that magical run in 2018. But the fact that he only has one year left on his contract at Oklahoma after the 2026-27 season, and the fact that he's now working for a new athletic director, makes Moser a reasonable candidate for any list like this. 
It's also worth noting that Moser has only made the NCAA Tournament once in five years at OU, and he's finished tied for 13th and tied for 11th in the SEC since the Sooners joined that league in advance of the 2024-25 season. Any similar finish in the conference and Oklahoma missing an expanded 76-team NCAA Tournament could convince first-year AD Roger Denny to make a move.
        
            
                Ranking college basketball coaches: UConn's Dan Hurley tops Houston's Kelvin Sampson, St. John's Rick Pitino
                
                    David Cobb                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Lamont Paris | South CarolinaRecord at school: 62-68 entering fifth seasonLast NCAA Tournament appearance at school: 2024South Carolina is one of the most challenging jobs in the SEC, if not the most challenging. But Paris is 6-30 in conference games over the past two seasons with first-round exits in the league tournament each year.
That's not good enough.South Carolina reportedly invested somewhere between $15 million and $17.5 million in this season's roster -- and yet KenPom still projects the Gamecocks to finish last in the SEC with a 4-14 record. Anything close to that, and it's hard to imagine Paris getting a sixth season. South Carolina has finished 12th or worse in the conference in three of his first four years and lost his only NCAA Tournament game at South Carolina by double digits to an Oregon team that was seeded worse and finished 55th at KenPom.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Mark Pope | Kentucky Record at school: 46-26 entering third seasonLast NCAA Tournament appearance at school: 2026Give Pope any normal Power-4 job, and he's fine. No issues. He might even get a contract extension. But Pope doesn't have any normal Power-4 job. What he has is arguably the most intense job in college basketball, if not all of basketball at any level in any country. So, sure, a trip to the Sweet 16 in Year 1 followed by a trip to the Round of 32 in Year 2 would be celebrated nearly everywhere other than Kentucky -- but at Kentucky it turns you into the face of this list and in need of better in Year 3 to ensure a Year 4.
The other problem for Pope is that he's following Calipari.The Hall of Famer set a high bar.Calipari went to the Elite Eight in Year 1 at UK, to the Final Four in Year 2, and never went consecutive years without making the Elite Eight for the first decade he had the job. Pope's first UK team finished tied for sixth in the SEC. His second finished tied for seventh. Calipari only finished outside of the top four of the SEC once in 15 years at Kentucky -- and that didn't come until Year 12. Different eras and all that; I get it. But UK fans still remember it and want seasons like those. And as Matt Norlander and I discussed on a recent episode of the Eye On College Basketball Podcast, if Pope doesn't deliver something this season closer to the type of season Calipari regularly delivered, that passionate fanbase that spans the state and then some won't be shy about telling first-year athletic director J Batt what they want him to do.

        
            
                NIL arms race: Matt Painter leads ranking of college basketball coaches outperforming their roster budgets
                
                    David Cobb                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Mike Young | Virginia Tech Record at school: 124-98 entering eighth seasonLast NCAA Tournament appearance at school: 2022Virginia Tech made the NCAA Tournament three straight years before Young took over, following Buzz Williams' five-year run that culminated in a trip to the 2019 Sweet 16. Since then, the Hokies have only made two NCAA Tournaments in seven years under Young. They're 0-2 in the Big Dance. And those losses were in 2021 and 2022, meaning Virginia Tech has missed four straight NCAA Tournaments, in part because the Hokies have finished no better than tied for eighth in the ACC in any of the previous four seasons.Did Young get an extension in July?Yes -- but it was only an extension through the end of the 2027-28 season. That's not an administration showing confidence in a coach as much as it's just an act of kindness. I personally have Virginia Tech finishing eighth in the ACC this season, which might be enough for the Hokies to make the NCAA Tournament, which might get Young another extension. But anything short of that could easily lead to the Hokies missing a fifth consecutive NCAA Tournament, and most believe that missing a fifth consecutive NCAA Tournament would lead to somebody other than Young coaching Virginia Tech next season.

title: Will Colts bench Daniel Jones? Shane Steichen backs struggling QB after loss to Vikings - CBS Sports
description: Anthony Richardson and Riley Leonard offer little evidence that either would represent an upgrade
body:
Anthony Richardson and Riley Leonard offer little evidence that either would represent an upgrade

    11:58 am ET

        Quarterback Daniel Jones was a primary reason why the Indianapolis Colts opened the 2025 season on a hot streak, but he is now a key factor in the team's dreadful start to 2026. Jones ranks among the NFL's least efficient passers through Week 7 and struggled mightily in the Colts' latest loss: A 16-10 rock fight with the Minnesota Vikings. Despite his rough first two months of the campaign, though, coach Shane Steichen said he has no plans to make a quarterback change.That leaves Jones entrenched in the lineup for a 2-5 team that ranks 25th in total offense per game."I have not thought about a quarterback change," Steichen said after the loss to Minnesota. "I've got a ton of faith in Daniel. The game plan today was to go in and run the football. Obviously, at the end, he had the interception. That happens in football."The interception in question was a game-sealer. Indianapolis had possession with 1:39 to play on Sunday and needed a touchdown to take a late and potentially decisive lead. Two plays into the Colts' final drive of the game, Jones threw a devastating pick to Vikings safety Harrison Smith. He finished the contest 13-for-22 for 108 yards and took four sacks.
Few quarterbacks have been able to move the ball with any kind of consistency against the ferocious Vikings defense, to be fair. But Jones was a uniquely favorable matchup for Minnesota, considering he has been one of the NFL's worst quarterbacks under pressure this season. The Vikings are the league's most proficient team at pressuring the signal-caller, and coordinator Brian Flores uncorked the pass rush to a historic extent in Week 7 by blitzing Jones on 85.2% of his dropbacks. That was the highest blitz rate by any defense in a game in the Next Gen Stats era (since 2016).Jones said it "means a lot" to have his coach's confidence after such a rough showing."It's my job to play well, to put the team in position to win games," Jones said. "I gotta do a better job of that. I certainly understand that. We all gotta go back to work. I gotta go back to work, see where I can be better."
Daniel Jones stats, rankingsAmong 33 qualified passersCategoryValueNFL rankPassing yards per game199.722ndCompletion %59.627thInterceptions7T-29thEPA per dropback-0.2030thPassing TDs per game0.6T-31stPasser rating69.431stWho would the Colts even turn to?The unfortunate reality for the Colts is that they might be better off with this version of Jones than with either Anthony Richardson or Riley Leonard as their starter. Richardson remains the backup in his fourth NFL season, while the Colts have been designating Leonard as inactive but keeping him available as the emergency third quarterback. Neither backup has any track record of productivity, and both have lower ceilings than Jones displayed in his breakout start to last season.Indianapolis declined Richardson's fifth-year option but could give him another look in the final year of his rookie contract. Anything the Colts get out of the former No. 4 overall pick would be a bonus at this point, because he is no longer part of the team's long-term plans following a massively disappointing start to his career in which he made just 15 starts over three years and threw more interceptions (13) than touchdowns (11) while completing only 50.6% of his throws. Richardson never developed as a passer and remains only a highly athletic rushing weapon.Leonard, in his second year as a former sixth-round pick, might not offer much more in the way of passing ability. He made five appearances and one start as a rookie and went 39-for-67 for 415 yards with two touchdowns and three interceptions. While he is also a running threat, the fact that he did not beat Richardson for the No. 2 job indicates the Notre Dame product is even less of an option.Colts face difficult decisions in 2027 and beyondOne of the final significant moves of Chris Ballard's tenure as general manager before the Colts fired him this month was to extend Jones on a two-year deal. It was a questionable signing in March, considering Jones was coming off a torn Achilles, and so far it has not paid off. Even worse, it ties Indianapolis to Jones through 2027 at a high price.Jones earns an average annual salary of $44 million and is guaranteed $60 million over the life of the two-year contract. He will carry a $46.8 million salary cap hit next season, so the Colts are likely committed to him as the starter for another year. The hope, of course, is that he will return to the form he showed at the start of 2025 as he becomes further removed from his Achilles tear. But if he does not, then he will be immensely expensive for what he is: One of the league's least productive starting quarterbacks.Richardson will likely be out of the picture next year, and Leonard is expendable with an annual salary of $1.1 million and effectively no dead cap hit should the Colts release him. Indianapolis could entirely retool the quarterback room behind Jones.If Indianapolis is not confident in Jones' ability to rebound next year, it could target a quarterback in the draft. This is where the Colts feel the ramifications of the poorly aged Sauce Gardner trade, because that deal leaves them without a first-round pick in 2027.

title: College basketball coach rankings: UConn's Dan Hurley tops Houston's Kelvin Sampson, St. John's Rick Pitino - CBS Sports

body:
The 2026 version of CBS Sports' annual Top 25 And 1 preseason coaches ranking features a nearly 20% churn rate, as five coaches who didn't make last year's list are crashing the party this time around. But the ranking will look familiar at the top.UConn's Dan Hurley is No. 1 for a third year in a row. In fact, this year's top three of Hurley, Kelvin Sampson (Houston) and Rick Pitino (St. John's) remains unchanged.  One of the top contenders to potentially crash that rarified air, Dusty May, left for the NBA after leading Michigan to a national championship. May's departure and Greg McDermott's retirement guaranteed there would be some attrition.Mark Pope (Kentucky), Chris Beard (Ole Miss) and Shaka Smart (Marquette) are the other three coaches who do not appear in this year's Top 25 and 1 coaches ranking after making the 2025 version. All three failed to meet expectations in 2025-26. With plenty of other great candidates waiting at the door, they have been displaced for now.As for big risers, Arizona's Tommy Lloyd and Illinois' Brad Underwood fit the bill. Both were ranked last year, but they made significant jumps this year after leading their programs to the 2026 Final Four.

        
            
                NIL arms race: Matt Painter leads ranking of college basketball coaches outperforming their roster budgets
                
                    David Cobb                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Here is our panel's collective ranking of the Top 25 and 1 college basketball coaches as the new season gets underway. Rankings determined by voting from CBS Sports' Gary Parrish, Matt Norlander, David Cobb, Cameron Salerno and Isaac Trotter. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
      1. Dan Hurley, UConn  Hurley guided UConn to its third national title game appearance in a four-year span before the Huskies ran into a historically dominant Michigan team on the season's final night. While Hurley fell just short of becoming the first coach since John Wooden to win three national championships in four years, he's presiding over a dynasty. At 53, he could keep it going for quite some time. He was the unanimous No. 1 choice by our panelists. (Last year: 1)  

                            
    
                                                
                    
      2. Kelvin Sampson, Houston  Sampson reached 30+ wins for a fifth consecutive season in 2025-26, as he guided Houston to a No. 2 seed in the NCAA Tournament. The Cougars fell in the Sweet 16, but Sampson has taken them past the first weekend in seven straight years. The only thing missing from the 71-year old's resume is a national title. Even if it never comes, his revitalization of Houston is Hall-of-Fame caliber. (Last year: 2)––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
                            
    
                                                
                    
    3. Rick Pitino, St. John'sPitino guided St. John's to a second straight outright Big East title and a second straight conference tournament title in 2025-26. He is 61-12 (36-4 Big East) over the past two years. At 74, he's as imposing of a presence today as he was while leading Providence to a Final Four at age 34. On the heels of a Sweet 16 appearance, could Pitino be primed for one more Final Four run? (Last year: 3)

                            
    
                                                
                    
    4. Todd Golden, FloridaFlorida didn't back up its 2025 national championship with another title. But the Gators won the SEC by three games in 2026, which is an achievement even the vaunted 2025 team can't claim. Now entering his fifth season, Golden has the AP poll's preseason No. 1 team and the analytics-backed coaching style to maximize its ample potential. At just 41, the former Saint Mary's guard could be a force on the sideline for decades to come. (Last year: 7)
                            
    
                                                
                    
    5. Matt Painter, PurduePainter's coaching excellence came further into focus with this month's deep dive from Matt Norlander and Isaac Trotter into how much teams are spending on their rosters. Purdue landed in the sixth of seven tiers, underscoring Painter's remarkable ability to do more with less. This could be something of a rebuilding year for the Boilermakers, but Painter's program never stays down long. (Last year: 5)
                            
    
                                                
                    
    6. Tommy Lloyd, ArizonaLloyd has won 80.4% of his games through five seasons and is coming off his best year yet. The Wildcats finished 36-3 while reaching the Final Four for the first time in 25 years. Arizona has become a prime destination for both international talent and highly touted freshmen. Lloyd pieced it all together perfectly last year with the best defensive team of his tenure. (Last year: 15)

                            
    
                                                
                    
    7. Tom Izzo, Michigan StateIn terms of his ability to produce great basketball teams, Izzo is aging like fine wine. He's 57-15 (32-8 Big Ten) over the past two seasons with a Sweet 16 and an Elite Eight. The Spartans exceeded expectations in both cases as Izzo reestablished Michigan State among the nation's top programs. His 2026-27 team enters the season ranked No. 6. Could it be his ninth Final Four team? (Last year: 8)
                            
    
                                                
                    
    8. Bill Self, KansasKansas no longer runs the Big 12 and has been eliminated on the first weekend of the NCAA Tournament in four consecutive years since winning the 2022 national title. Even still, some of the leanest years of Self's 24-year tenure would be considered great by the standards of almost any other coach. When you've won two national championships and 16 Big 12 titles, the definition of success can get skewed. (Last year: 4)
                            
    
                                                
                    
    9. Jon Scheyer, DukeBecause Scheyer spent 13 years in the public eye as a player or assistant under Mike Krzyzewski, it can be easy to forget he's still a 39-year old first time head coach with just four seasons under his belt. In that context, his 70-7 (38-2 ACC) record over the past two years is even more impressive. He hasn't delivered a national championship yet. But it's only a matter of time. (Last year: 11)

                            
    
                                                
                    
    10. Nate Oats, AlabamaOats is presiding over the greatest era of Alabama basketball history as he enters his eighth season. The Crimson Tide have made six straight NCAA Tournament appearances and have advanced beyond the first weekend five times. His trademark up-tempo style perennially produces one of the nation's top offenses and NBA Draft picks. (Last year: 6)
                            
    
                                                
                    
      11. Mark Few, GonzagaFew is shepherding Gonzaga into a new era, as the Bulldogs join a revitalized Pac-12 for the 2026-27 season after running the WCC for 27 years under his direction. No coach is more synonymous with a program than Few is with Gonzaga, which has grown from a mid-major into a perennial power under his direction. (Last year: 9)
                            
    
                                                
                    
      12. Brad Underwood, IllinoisUnderwood grinded through the junior college and low-major ranks before finally getting a high-major head coaching opportunity in his 50s. His Illinois rebuild, which started in the pre-portal era, didn't happen overnight. But Underwood kept chipping away and got the Illini to the 2026 Final Four. Few, if any, are better at mining the international waters for talent. (Last year: 19)

                            
    
                                                
                    
      13. John Calipari, ArkansasEntering his third season at Arkansas, Calipari is winning the breakup with Kentucky. He's made two Sweet 16s with the Razorbacks, and his third team is ranked No. 12 in the AP preseason poll. At 67, Calipari continues attracting elite talent and letting it shine.  (Last year: 14)
                            
    
                                                
                    
      14. TJ Otzelberger, Iowa StateOtzelberger has sculpted five straight top-15 defenses over his first five seasons at Iowa State while reaching three Sweet 16s. He doesn't have a top-line budget, but he finds the right fits and then builds gritty winners. His sixth team is beginning the season at No. 6 in KenPom's rating and should compete for the Big 12 title. (Last year: 21)
                            
    
                                                
                    
      15. Grant McCasland, Texas TechMcCasland is 74-31 (38-18 Big 12) through three seasons at Texas Tech with an Elite Eight appearance (2025). If not for a season-ending injury to star forward JT Toppin, last year's squad was primed to make another deep run. (Last year: 18)

                            
    
                                                
                    
      16. Rick Barnes, TennesseeTennessee has made four Elite Eight appearances in program history. Barnes is responsible for three of them over the past three seasons alone. Those runs have quieted the chatter about his March struggles as he's built the Volunteers into one of the nation's steadiest winners. (Last year: 13)
                            
    
                                                
                    
      17. Scott Drew, BaylorDrew inherited a moribund program in 2003 and built a national champion in less than two decades. The past five seasons since the Bears' 2021 title haven't been as fruitful. But even if he never nears the mountaintop again, Drew's build at Baylor will go down as one of the greatest in college basketball history.  (Last year: 10)––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

                            
    
                                                
                    
      18. Mick Cronin, UCLACronin is entering Year 8 at UCLA after spending the last two years guiding the Bruins through their transition from the Pac-12 to Big Ten. UCLA is 47-23 (26-14)  during that span with a pair of second round NCAA Tournament exits. (Last year: 23)
                            
    
                                                
                    
    19. Sean Miller, TexasMiller's first season at Texas resulted in a Sweet 16 run after the Longhorn barely squeaked into the field. But this is a vote of confidence in what he's building after successful runs at Xavier (twice) and Arizona. (Last year: unranked)
                            
    
                                                
                    
      20. Ben McCollum, IowaMcCollum is proof that great coaches can come from any level. After a prolific 15-year run at Division II Northwest Missouri State, he's entering his third season as a Division I coach with four NCAA Tournament wins already under his belt. (Last year: 26)

                            
    
                                                
                    
      21. Mark Byington, VanderbiltVanderbilt's two-year turnaround under Byington is a sight to behold after he inherited a 9-23 team following the 2023-24 season. He is 47-22 with a pair of NCAA Tournament appearances after taking James Madison to the second round of the Big Dance in 2024. (Last year: unranked)
                            
    
                                                
                    
      22. Ryan Odom, VirginiaOdom inherited a 15-win team and won 30 games in his first season after arriving from VCU. The architect of UMBC's historic 2018 upset of No. 1 seed Virginia is now leading the Cavaliers back to national prominence. (Last year: unranked)
                            
    
                                                
                    
      23. Pat Kelsey, LouisvilleKelsey will need to go past the first weekend of the NCAA Tournament sooner or later. But he's totally revitalized a Louisville program that fell into disrepair under Kenny Payne. The Cardinals have loaded up to make a run this season. (Last year: 20)
                            
    
                                                
                    
    24. Randy Bennett, Arizona StateAfter 25 years at Saint Mary's, Bennett is now trying his hand with a high-major program. Arizona State is a challenging job, but so was Saint Mary's when Bennett took over and built it up from nothing. (Last year: 24) ––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
                            
    
                                                
                    
      25. Jai Lucas, MiamiLucas burst onto the scene with a 26-9 (13-5 ACC) debut campaign. As a young, first-time head coach he was a total wild card entering the year. The 37-year old is quickly putting most questions to rest. (Last year: unranked)––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
                            
    
                                                
                    
     	And 1: Fred Hoiberg, NebraskaWhat Hoiberg has done over the past three seasons stands out, highlighted by the first two NCAA Tournament wins in Nebraska history in 2026. It's the first time in program history Nebraska has won 20+ . (Last year: unranked)
